newsitem.title: USA: Holiday jars weekly US mortgage application data.
newsitem.headline: Holiday jars weekly US mortgage application data.

text.p: A holiday-shortened week likely damped U.S. mortgage applications in the week ended July 4, according to a Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) economist.
"There is one less day in the (business) week, which means there is 20-percent less time" to conduct business with a mortgage banker, said Brian Carey, an MBA economist.
While total applications declined by 15.6 percent in the week ended July 4, the seasonally adjusted market index rose five percent and the seasonally adjusted purchase index rose 7.4-percent.
Carey noted that seasonally adjusted data took the holiday-shortened week into consideration.

The MBA economist predicted that refinancings would climb following U.S. Treasury interest rate declines. "I would expect a pick-up in refinancings in next week's survey," he said, noting that seasonally adjusted, the refinancing index could climb to 450.0 in the week ended July 11 from 414.6 in the latest reporting week.
But Carey does not believe that a major rise in refinancings is on the horizon.

Homeowners with fixed-rate mortgages had a chance to refinance in 1992 and 1993, he said. Pools of loans originated in 1995 and 1996 will not likely be refinanced because it is not cost effective, he stated.
Meanwhile, adjustable-rate mortgage products are seeing some heightened refinancing activity, the MBA economist said.
"ARMs are prepaying at a faster rate than in past years. A fully indexed ARM is more expensive than a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage product," said Carey.
Some holders of adjustable-rate loans may be paying as much as 8.4 percent -- 55 basis points more than the 30-year fixed-rate product with an 7.85 percent rate, he said.
How does that affect a homeowner's purse? For a $100,000 home, Carey said, that difference amounts to about $35 each month.
